questions.text: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?
questions.solution:
Bottom-up parsers build the parse tree from the leaves up to the root using reductions: shift-reduce parsers, operator precedence parser and the LR family (LR(0), SLR, LALR, CLR).

Predictive parser and LL(1) parser are top-down parsers.

Answer: Shift-reduce Parser, LR Parser

questions.text: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be two events in a probability space with [latex]P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5 [/latex], and [latex]P(A \cap B)=0.1 [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Independence: [latex]P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=0.3-0.1=0.2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A\cup B)=0.3\ne0.4[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.7[/latex] and [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=0.2[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The two events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are independent
[latex]P(A \cup B)=0.7[/latex]
[latex]P\left(A \cap B^c\right)=0.2 [/latex], where [latex]B^c [/latex] is the complement of the event [latex]B [/latex]
[latex]P\left(A^c \cap B^c\right)=0.4 [/latex], where [latex]A^c [/latex] and [latex]B^c [/latex] are the complements of the events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex], respectively

questions.text: Consider the circuit shown below where the gates may have propagation delays. Assume that all signal transitions occur instantaneously and that wires have no delays. Which of the following statements about the circuit is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
The circuit computes [latex]Y=X\cdot\overline{X}[/latex].

- No delays: [latex]X\cdot\overline{X}=0[/latex] always [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Y is always 0 (option 1 TRUE, option 2 FALSE).
- X goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1: the AND gate sees X = 1 immediately, but the NOT output is still 1 until its delay passes. For that short time both inputs are 1, so Y gives a transient 1 (glitch) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- X goes 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0: the direct input becomes 0 immediately, so Y stays 0 no matter what the NOT output does [latex]\text{---}[/latex] no transient, FALSE.

Answer: Y is always 0 with no delays; with delays Y can have a transient 1 after X goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: With no propagation delays, the output Y is always logic Zero
With no propagation delays, the output Y is always logic One

With propagation delays, the output Y can have a transient logic One after X
transitions from logic Zero to logic One

With propagation delays, the output Y can have a transient logic Zero after X
transitions from logic One to logic Zero

questions.text: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_P [/latex] denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] to [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_Q [/latex] denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly (to avoid confusion with old segments and for security) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE; it is not always 0.
- A SYN segment consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges with the next expected number: [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]N_Q=N_P[/latex] is false).

Answer: [latex]N_P[/latex] is chosen randomly by P; [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is chosen randomly by [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex]
The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is always 0 for a new connection
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P [/latex]
The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P+1 [/latex]

questions.text: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: this is exactly the definition of forwarding (bypassing) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: a value available at the output of MEM (e.g. a loaded value) can be fed to the EX input of a later instruction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 3: forwarding cannot remove every stall. Example: load followed immediately by an instruction using the loaded value still needs 1 stall (load-use hazard) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 4: forwarding needs extra hardware (extra paths, multiplexers, hazard detection logic) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options:
In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an
earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction

In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the
input of the EX stage of the next instruction
Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls

Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the
pipeline stages
